items: Create a complete food inventory by listing every food your child reliably eats, being specific about brands and preparations like 'chicken nuggets' vs 'chicken in any form'.
Categorize each food in your inventory as safe (willingly eaten), maybe (sometimes accepted), or never (consistently refused) to map your child's current diet profile.
Analyze your food inventory for patterns in texture, color, brand, temperature, and processing level to understand what drives your child's food preferences.
Determine where your child falls on the selective eating spectrum: typical picky eating (15-30 foods), significant selective eating (under 15 foods), or severe ARFID-risk (under 10 foods).
Watch for texture sensitivities like gagging on smooth foods or refusing mushy items to identify which food textures trigger genuine discomfort rather than defiance.
Observe whether your child rejects foods based on visual appearance, such as refusing all green foods regardless of taste or avoiding certain colors entirely.
Track your child's temperature preferences by noting whether they accept foods only when warm, cold, or at room temperature to expand their diet systematically.
Document smell sensitivities by noting which strong-smelling foods like fish, eggs, or cruciferous vegetables cause genuine aversive reactions in your child.
Monitor your child's growth curve at pediatrician visits to identify if their growth has flattened or if they've lost weight, which may indicate nutritional concerns.
Request blood work from your pediatrician to check for nutritional deficiencies, particularly iron, which is commonly low in children with restricted diets.
Watch for extreme anxiety around food such as panic, gagging, or vomiting at the sight of new foods, which may require professional feeding therapy support.
Recognize when selective eating is causing significant family conflict or parental depression and seek professional support rather than struggling alone.
